Cordial

KOR-jul -- from Latin cor ('heart') -- related to cardiac, courage, and accord, though cor itself isn't a standalone English word. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

To be cordial is to be warm, comforting, and friendly.

Even after losing the election, the two candidates shook hands and exchanged a cordial word of congratulations.

Worked Example

The rival law firms kept their relationship strictly cordial -- polite handshakes and pleasant small talk at conferences -- even while competing fiercely for the same clients.

Cordial describes a warmth that is genuinely friendly but often somewhat formal or professional -- people can be cordial while still being rivals or strangers, unlike close friends who are simply "warm" toward each other.

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

Where it sits · how much real warmth shows through — polite → cordial → genial

polite vs. cordial: Polite describes basic good manners, sometimes without much real warmth.

genial vs. cordial: Genial goes further than cordial, describing someone naturally warm, cheerful, and easy to be around.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — cord-

root — cord-: heart (Latin cor -- not a standalone English word, but the root of cardiac, courage, and accord)

suffix — -ial

suffix — -ial: having the qualities of; pertaining to

Put it together

Put it together: Cordial traces back to the Latin word cor, meaning 'heart.' That root doesn't survive as its own English word, but you can hear it hiding inside cardiac (relating to the heart), courage (originally 'to act from the heart'), and accord (being 'of one heart,' or in agreement).

Strength Check

Word Choice

Cordial suggests warmth with a touch of formality -- perfectly friendly, but not necessarily deeply personal. Two diplomats can have a cordial relationship without being close friends.
